clinicalPearls: Defined by persistent marked eosinophilia (greater than 1.5 x 10^9/L on repeated testing or marked tissue eosinophilia) with end-organ damage and exclusion of secondary causes.
Recognised variants include myeloproliferative (often FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion), lymphocytic (an aberrant clonal T-cell population driving interleukin-5), idiopathic and overlap forms.
FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive disease is exquisitely responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.
Cardiac involvement (Loffler endocarditis, endomyocardial fibrosis and mural thrombi) is the major cause of morbidity and mortality.
Other affected organs include the skin, lungs, gastrointestinal tract and nervous system, with peripheral neuropathy and thromboembolic stroke.
Raised serum tryptase and vitamin B12 point towards the myeloproliferative variant.
Exclude secondary eosinophilia from parasites, drugs, allergy, malignancy, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and adrenal insufficiency.
Corticosteroids are first line for non-PDGFRA disease, with anti-interleukin-5 therapy (mepolizumab) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors as targeted options.
reference.pathophysiology: Hypereosinophilic syndrome is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by sustained overproduction of eosinophils that infiltrate and damage tissues through release of granule proteins (major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein), cytokines and pro-thrombotic mediators. In the myeloproliferative variant, clonal expansion is driven by fusion tyrosine kinases, classically FIP1L1-PDGFRA; in the lymphocytic variant an aberrant clonal T-cell population secretes interleukin-5 driving reactive eosinophilia. Cardiac damage evolves through acute necrotic, thrombotic and fibrotic stages, producing restrictive endomyocardial fibrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia and other myeloid neoplasms
Allergic or atopic disease and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
additionalInvestigations: Repeated full blood count with eosinophil quantification and blood film
Testing for FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other PDGFRA, PDGFRB and FGFR1 rearrangements
Peripheral blood T-cell immunophenotyping and T-cell receptor clonality
Serum tryptase, vitamin B12 and IgE
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics
Stool and serology for parasites and exclusion of secondary causes
redFlags: Cardiac involvement with heart failure, a new murmur, raised troponin or mural thrombus
Rapidly rising eosinophil count with systemic deterioration
reference.prognosis: Prognosis has improved markedly with modern targeted therapy: FIP1L1-PDGFRA disease responds excellently to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, while outcome in other variants depends largely on the extent of cardiac and neurological damage.
pitfalls: Missing FIP1L1-PDGFRA, a highly treatable cause, before committing to corticosteroids alone
Overlooking cardiac involvement because symptoms lag behind structural damage
Failing to exclude Strongyloides before immunosuppression
Confusing the syndrome with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis or reactive eosinophilia
references: World Health Organization classification of haematolymphoid tumours
